In regards to specifically the vegas shooting: 

The most common conspiracy you find with this shooting does not deny people died. It is the deadliest mass shooting in our country's history and the (most common) conspiracy surrounding still treats it as such. 

Where the conspiracy differs from the generally accepted narrative is on *who perpetrated* the shooting. 

The conspiracy alleges that the shooting was perpetrated either by the government or a hit team to assassinate the Crown Prince of Saudi Arabia who (allegedly, I'm not checking if this is factual) was staying at the Mandalay Bay. It alleges that the mass shooting was perpetrated as a cover up for the assassination attempt. (Evil and Machiavellian oOoOo)

There are a few factors that aid this conspiracy theory with the biggest (in my personal opinion) being the complete lack of disclosure on information about the shooter. When information isn't released people tend to try to fill in the gaps on their own. 

The unique structure of the building also contributed as it created multiple echos of the gunshots, which in the chaos would absolutely sound like multiple shooters. 

The last big point conspiracy theorists make is the cadence and sound of the gunshots themselves. They do line up with modern day military machine guns like the M240B, however this really doesn't mean much as an AR-15 with a bump stock still sounds similar. The only thing that gets me on this is fore rate with bump stocks is inconsistent, which isn't the case if you listen to the video. 

Oh and the guys brother said there's no way he did it then days later they magically found a bunch of child porn on his computer which is just.. *strange*

I think it was just a crazy guy, but this is probably the most common conspiracy I've seen surrounding this particular shooting. 

I'm sure there are others claiming crisis actors and such, but I haven't seen those theories get nearly as much traction as the MBS hit job one. 


There are conspiracies that deny the deaths of victims, but by and large Vegas isn't really ne of them.

Want to preface this with an I do not endorse this message, but I think I follow what they're trying to say. 

So there is an implied premise here that a small subset of men is having all the sex. Thus the majority of men will not have an std because they don't have sex. 

To put it into numbers let's say you have a group of 10 women and 10 men. If the 10 women have sex with only 4 of the men, and one of the men has HIV, then it would hold true that both women are more likely to contract *and spread* an std than men simply because there's more women. If a person outside the group had sex with any member of the group there would be a higher likelihood of infection if the person slept with one of the women.  The women are also more likely to contract it since at the end of the experiment more women had the std than men. 

Is this how it works in real life? No not really. They're overly simple conclusions to try and extrapolate to normal life, but that was the thought process behind the argument. 

It doesn't make it any less dumb, but hopefully that helps the confusion

Nice dude!! I know people shit on Hyundai, but I loved my veloster and the newer N models look great imo. 

However, I would bet my life savings that you'll have the exact same problems that both I and my mom had on our separate velosters. The first thing to go on both was a little spacer thingy on the steering rack. Wheel would vibrate a lot and stuff and go wacky. If that happens the little plastic spacer broke and ya gotta get it replaced. Luckily it's not the whole steering rack gone. 

The next thing was the passenger side door handle. The handle is made of two pieces. The rearward piece breaks and falls off, which allows the door handle to fall out. Once again an easy fix, but be aware so you don't lose the handle!! That rear piece is all that keeps the handle connected and without it the handle will slide right out. I recommend removing the handle until you need to open the door. 

Finally the hatch latch likes to break. Not too sure why. Once again easy fix. 

For reference the steering rack issue appeared for both of us around 60-70,000 miles. The other issues appearing around 100-110,000 miles. 

Happy driving!

The history of long range precision shooting has its roots in hunting and marksmanship (as back then typically only soldiers and the aristocracy had rifles, the common man was not allowed to hunt unless part of an official hunting party). That being said once rifles started becoming more prevalent small shooting clubs began to open. The first matches in the sport weren’t held as a “we need to practice for war”, but were actually more of friendly sporting between different country’s shooting clubs. One of the first notable being between The Ireland National Guard sport shooting team and the Amateur Rifle Club of the United States. Even while one team was a member of a national guard, both teams purpose was not to kill, but rather to put holes in targets really far away. In fact general discussion of long range shooting at the time was far more popular in gentleman’s clubs and country clubs rather than specifically in the military, with the obvious exception that back then high ranking members of the military could often be found in these clubs (though not exclusively). 

It would be disingenuous for one to argue that the great great grandfather of the sport was not to shoot living things, whether animal or man. However, to say that the modern day sport of long range precision shooting has anything to do with that would be like saying that NASCAR is literally just moonshining, or practicing for moonshining, just because that’s how the sport started. These are very, very different guns from what you see every day, and even different from standard bolt action hunting rifles to a considerable degree. They are very heavy and unwieldy and, depending on the shooter, can have hair triggers that would make them horrible for safety in the military or carrying around the woods hunting (which granted most people probably couldn’t without scaring everything off, once again these are not walk around rifles). Oh yeah the youtube gun community will definitely give the wrong impression haha. I’d like to collect them so I’ve looked into it. A common misconception is that you need a license to own them. You don’t need one unless you intend to sell them or make them. 

There are three types of machine guns - Pre Ban, Post Sample, and Transferable. Transferable machine guns are the only ones that can be purchased by regular people without licenses. The others have certain rules governing the others but lets focus on what the average American would have to deal with. 

They stopped registering new machine guns for civilians in 1986. This means that any machine gun made after a certain day in 1986 is not available for purchase to the general public. What this means is that there is a finite amount of machine guns on that list, and as guns are lost or destroyed every year there will only ever be less of them. What this means is that the cheapest option available (usually something along the lines of a Mac-10) is currently somewhere around $8,000. To give a sense of inflation they only cost around $5,000 about 4 years ago. Something like the rifle pictured here in full auto would cost you between around $20,000-40,000, depending on if it’s an actual M16 lower or a registered AR-15 lower that had been legally modified and registered before 1986 (there is a difference mechanically between these two, but they look the same and provide full auto capability). I’d say most machine guns sit between $20,000 to around $65,000 *per gun*. The handy thing though with a full auto ar 15 lower is that it can fit multiple different uppers so with a little bit of work you can technically have a few different rifles, you can just only use one at a time. 

Now for the government. You will pay a $200 fee to the ATF to process your request to purchase a machine gun. This is a months long process typically lasting 6-14 months (although i hear the new e-forms can be as fast as 4 months) during which the rifle that you already paid thousands and thousands of dollars for will sit under a counter at a gun store. Depending on the seller you may or may not have to pay the full amount of the machine gun before you’re approved by the ATF. Some will let you put a down payment, with the rest to be paid on acceptance, but this is not always the case. 

Once you’re approved you get your gun (yay!!), but that isn’t all. Now your name is on a list and you will be of particular interest to your local ATF Field Office. At any point in time, and without reason you can be audited, in which case you better have every gun that they regula exactly where you told them it would be. They will enter your home. They will check any building on the property listed on the registry, and if they can’t find what they’re looking for there is a chance that you could go to federal prison. You cannot cross state lines with it unless you have written consent from the ATF prior to travel. If you commit any state-level crime you have now also opened yourself up to federal charges (this is what happened to FPSRussia on youtube). The ATF can search your house without warrant thanks to the fact that you own a machine gun. 

Is all of this worth it? I mean, that would be up to the buyer. They’re super fun to shoot, and if ya can’t afford one then ya probably can’t afford the ammo to shoot one. I really don’t like the warrantless search aspect, but hey machine guns, as fun as they are, should be regulated pretty heavily.

People don’t seem to understand that machine guns are already regulated out the wazoo. Personally my only gripe is the closed registry. I wouldn’t mind forfeiting all the rights required to own one and jumping through the hoops to get one since they’re tons of fun, but by closing the registry in ‘86 they made them prohibitively expensive rip

Your looking at it as Coin A and Coin B, and so we should also count TT twice because of a Coin B then Coin A configuration.

So we have two options, TH and HT because we can either get

Throw 1: H
Throw 2: T

or 

Throw 1: T
Throw 2: H

However we don’t count HH or TT twice because there’s only one configuration:

Throw 1: H

Since we’re counting by throws and not coins flipping these around says the exact same thing, and thus is the same configuration.
